coreTruths.title: Malocclusion is variation from ideal, not a disease — treatment is justified by aesthetics, function, and risk-benefit, not by oral health alone
coreTruths.broaderContext: Orthodontics sits apart from caries and perio because the target is not pathology. That changes how cases are selected, what is offered, and what counts as a good outcome.
coreTruths.body:
## Malocclusion is variation, not disease

Malocclusion is variation from an anatomically ideal occlusion, not a disease state [1]. Crowding affects roughly 60% of people, so most patients carry some degree of it. That framing matters because it shifts the conversation away from cure and toward whether treatment is worth it for this individual.

## Plaque control beats alignment for oral health

Motivation, not tooth alignment, drives plaque levels [2]. Straight teeth do not protect the periodontium on their own. So the main reasons to treat are aesthetics and function, not OH. Functional reasons include traumatic deep overbite, increased overjet with incompetent lips (trauma risk), and labial crowding of a lower incisor that is starting to lose periodontal support [2].

## Treatment carries real risks that have to be weighed

Even with good OH, a small loss of periodontal attachment is common, and around 1 to 2 mm of root resorption is associated with fixed appliance treatment [3]. Decalcification follows frequent sugar intakes between meals. The benefit has to outweigh those risks before treatment goes ahead.

## IOTN exists because need is hard to standardise

Perceived need is shaped by social and cultural factors, so the IOTN was developed to standardise how need is measured [4]. The dental health component grades by the single worst feature using MOCDO (Missing teeth, Overjet, Crossbite, Displacement, Overbite) [5]. The aesthetic component uses a ten-photo ranking scale. Together they let a clinician justify treatment on something more solid than a hunch.

citations.quote: Orthodontics has been defined as that branch of dentistry concerned with growth of the face, development of the dentition, and prevention and correction of occlusal anomalies. Ortho (from Greek) = straight. Malocclusion is not a disease—it is variation from ideal occlusion.

Research shows that individual motivation has more effect upon the presence of plaque than alignment of the teeth; therefore, the main indications for orthodontic Rx are aesthetics and function. Functional reasons for Rx include deep traumatic overbite, ↑ o/j especially if the lips are incompetent (↑ risk of trauma), and labial crowding of a lower incisor (as this reduces periodontal support labially).

Even with good OH, a small loss of periodontal attachment is common and with poor OH this will be i. Decalcification will occur if there are frequent sugar intakes between meals. Around 1–2mm of root resorption is associated with FA Rx and in at-risk patients (those with shortened/blunt root shapes) this risk may be i. Therefore, the potential benefits of orthodontic Rx must be sufficient to counter-balance these risks.

While it is accepted that severe malocclusion may affect self-esteem and psychological well-being, the impact of more minor anomalies and, indeed, perceived need are influenced by social and cultural factors. The Index of Orthodontic Treatment Need (IOTN) has been developed to try to standardize and quantify this difficult issue

The dental health component of IOTN has five categories of Rx need, ranging from little need to very great need. A patient’s grade is determined by recording the single worst feature of their malocclusion. ‘MOCDO’ is helpful when assessing dental health component as it provides a hierarchy of severity—Missing teeth; Overjet; Crossbite; Displacement; Overbite.

coreTruths.title: The lower arch sits in a zone of soft-tissue stability — plan treatment around its current position
coreTruths.broaderContext: Soft tissues set the boundary for what tooth positions hold long-term. Working with that envelope, not against it, is the rule that prevents most orthodontic relapse.
coreTruths.body:
## The lower arch defines the starting point

The lower arch lies in a zone of relative stability between the lips, cheeks, and tongue, so in most cases its current position is maintained as the anchor for the rest of the plan [1]. The first decision is whether the lower arch is crowded enough to warrant extractions. Once the lower arch is settled, the upper arch is positioned around it to achieve a Class I incisor relationship [2].

## Moving lower incisors out of their envelope is unstable

Proclining lower incisors out of the soft-tissue envelope is unstable in most cases [3]. Active proclination is a specialist call. The exception worth knowing: in some Class II/2 cases the LLS is trapped behind the ULS and freeing it with a biteplane can let the lowers procline to a new stable position [4].

## Skeletal pattern decides difficulty, soft tissues decide stability

In the majority of cases the skeletal pattern determines the difficulty of treatment, while the soft tissues determine whether the end result holds [5]. So a Class II/1 with the increased overjet caused by upper proclination has a better prognosis than the same overjet caused by lower retroclination, because the upper incisors can be retracted back within the control of the lower lip [6].

## Watch the lip-trap, vertical extremes, and obtuse naso-labial angle

Grossly incompetent lips, vertical proportions at either extreme, and an obtuse naso-labial angle all flag a less stable result [7]. An obtuse naso-labial angle gets worse as the overjet is reduced because the upper lip loses support [7]. None of those are absolute contraindications, but they are reasons to refer or to lower expectations on stability.

citations.quote: This lies in a zone of relative stability between the lips, cheeks, and tongue; therefore, in most cases it is advisable to maintain its current position. This gives a starting point around which to plan Rx.

Next, the position of the upper arch can be planned to achieve a Class I incisor relationship. This usually requires positioning, in the mind’s eye, the 3 into a Class I relationship with 3 (in corrected position if LLS crowded).

Proclination of lower incisors. Movement of the lower incisors from their position of stability within the soft tissue envelope is unstable in most cases. Active proclination should only be attempted by the experienced orthodontist, who will be better able to judge those cases where this is indicated.

In some Class II/2 cases, the LLS teeth are trapped by the ↑ o/b behind the ULS. Freeing them by, e.g. provision of an upper removable appliance (URA) with a biteplane, may allow the lower incisors to spontaneously procline to a new stable position. This is one of the few situations where proclination (within reason!) of the LLS is stable.
In the majority of cases, the skeletal pattern will determine the difficulty of Rx and the soft tissues will influence stability of the end result.

Where the lips are incompetent, the way an anterior oral seal is achieved will influence incisor position; e.g. if the lower lip is drawn up behind the upper incisors this may have contributed to the ↑ o/j, but if the incisors can be retracted within control of the lower lip at the end of Rx the prognosis for stability is i.
Beware: Obtuse naso-labial angle as o/j ↓ will further reduce lip support. Grossly incompetent lips as stability is compromised. Significantly ↑ or ↓ vertical proportions.

coreTruths.title: Growth is a treatment lever — timing dictates what is achievable
coreTruths.broaderContext: Bone, soft tissues, and tooth eruption are all moving targets in a child. Timing the intervention against that movement is what makes some corrections possible at all.
coreTruths.body:
## Most ortho waits for the early permanent dentition

Most orthodontic treatment does not start until the early permanent dentition, when canines and premolars have erupted. At that stage tooth movement is faster, appliances are tolerated better, and growth can still be used to drive sagittal or vertical change [1]. The exception worth knowing is protraction facemask therapy for Class III, which achieves more skeletal change at age 8 to 9 than later [1].

## Class II responds to growth more reliably than Class III

Mandibular growth predominates during the teenage years, so a greater proportion of Class II than Class III problems is amenable to orthodontic correction [2]. In practice, growing Class II patients often get a phase of functional appliance therapy followed by fixed appliances with or without extractions [2]. Class III tends to get worse with growth, which is why a positive overbite at the end of treatment matters so much for retention [3].

## Functional appliances ride the growth wave

Functional appliances harness forward mandibular growth to correct Class II by restraining the maxilla and pushing the mandible forward [4]. The change is roughly 25% skeletal and 75% dental, and the long-term skeletal gain is small (an extra 1 to 2 mm of mandibular growth in the short term) [5]. Success runs around 80% in growing patients [6]. Three keys: a cooperative patient, favourable growth (so coincide with the pubertal growth spurt), and a confident operator [7].

## In adults, the lever is gone

In adults, lack of growth, increased perio risk, worn or missing teeth, and slower tooth movement narrow what orthodontics can achieve alone [8]. Adults with severe skeletal problems often need surgery rather than camouflage.

citations.quote: Most orthodontic Rx is not started until the early 2° dentition, when the canines and premolars have erupted. At this stage, the response to orthodontic forces is more rapid, appliances are better tolerated, and, most importantly, growth can be utilized to help effect sagittal or vertical change. However, there is some evidence that protraction facemask therapy for Class III malocclusions achieves more skeletal change around age 8–9yrs than in older children.

Because mandibular growth predominates during the teenage years, a greater proportion of Class II than Class III skeletal problems is amenable to orthodontic correction. Research would suggest that the amount of growth modification that can be achieved is limited, but every little helps and in practice the majority of growing children in this category are treated by a combination of growth modification and camouflage. This usually takes the form of an initial phase of functional appliance therapy in the early permanent dentition, followed by FA ± extractions.
Class III malocclusions tend to become worse with growth.

In the average child, the face grows forward relative to the cranial base and mandibular growth predominates. Functional appliances help to harness this change to correct Class II malocclusions by a restraining effect on the maxilla and maxillary teeth and a forward pressure on the mandible and mandibular teeth.

Research would suggest that changes seen are 25% skeletal and 75% dental. Optimizing of mandibular growth. The evidence would suggest that in the short term an extra 1–2mm mandibular growth results, however, in the long term that overall gain is small.
Functional appliances are successful in around 80% of growing patients.

Cooperative and keen patient. Remember cooperation is finite. Favourable growth; therefore should coincide Rx with pubertal growth spurt. Confident operator, so that the child believes the appliance will work and will persevere with wearing it.
In adults, lack of growth, ↑ risk of periodontal disease, worn, damaged, and missing teeth, and slower tooth movement will limit the type of malocclusion that can be managed by orthodontics alone.

coreTruths.title: Anchorage is Newton's third law in the mouth — every active force creates an equal reaction that has to be planned for
coreTruths.broaderContext: Tooth movement is mechanics, not magic. Forgetting that the anchor teeth move too is the most common reason orthodontic plans drift off target.
coreTruths.body:
## Every active force has an equal and opposite reaction

To every force there is an equal and opposite reaction [1]. In orthodontics, the resistance to unwanted movement of the anchor teeth is called anchorage [1]. When canines are retracted into a premolar extraction space, the molars feel an equal forward pull. The amount they drift forward depends on their root surface area and the force applied [2].

## Anchorage has to be planned, not improvised

If 75 to 100% of the extraction space is needed for planned tooth movement, anchorage demands are high and have to be reinforced from the start [3]. Anchorage loss usually comes from underestimating that demand at the planning stage, over-activating springs, moving too many teeth at once, or poor patient compliance [3].

## Reinforcement options scale with the demand

Within the same arch, anchorage is reinforced by including more teeth in the anchor unit [4]. Across arches, intermaxillary elastics transfer reaction from one arch to the other [5]. Transpalatal and lingual arches link the molars and resist forward drift [6]. Headgear adds an extra-oral force, with direction tailored to vertical proportions: hi-pull for increased vertical, cervical pull for reduced [7].

## TADs change the calculus

Temporary anchorage devices give skeletal anchorage that does not depend on patient compliance and have widened the range of malocclusions treatable by orthodontics alone [8]. Reported success rates sit around 86.5% [8]. Self-drilling screws are now standard because they are simple to place and remove, and forces under 250 g are typical [9]. If a screw contacts a root, healing tends to occur by cementum [10].

## Headgear safety is non-negotiable

Reported cases of eye damage, including blindness, mean headgear must be used with at least two safety mechanisms to prevent facebow displacement or recoil [11]. If an eye injury occurs, immediate ophthalmology referral is required [11].

citations.quote: To every force there is an equal and opposite reaction. In orthodontic Rx, the resistance to unwanted tooth movement is called anchorage and also needs to be considered when planning Rx.

Anchorage is defined as the source of resistance to the reaction from the active component(s) in an appliance. In practice, it is the balance between the applied force and the available space, e.g. in a case where 3|3 are being retracted following extraction of 4|4, an equal, but opposite force will also be acting on 65|56. The amount of forward movement of these anchor teeth will depend largely upon their root surface area and the force used.

Failure to appreciate fully the anchorage requirements at Rx planning stage (generally if 75–100% of space generated from extractions is required for planned tooth movement, anchorage requirements are high). Active force exceeding available anchorage (often due to over-activation or too many teeth being moved at a time). Poor patient compliance.
Intra-maxillary (teeth in same arch) This is achieved by including the maximum number of teeth in the anchorage unit.
Inter-maxillary (teeth in opposing arch) This is achieved by running elastics from one arch to the other during FA Rx.
Transpalatal and lingual arches By virtue of linking the upper molars, a palatal arch limits their forward movement and thereby ↑ anchorage, and vice versa for the lingual arch.

The direction of pull can be selected according to the malocclusion with an overall direction of pull above the occlusal plane for patients with ↑ vertical proportions (hi-pull) and vice versa for ↓ vertical proportions (cervical pull). For EO anchorage, 250g for 10h/day should suffice. For EO traction (i.e. using the headgear force to achieve movement rather than just resist it), forces in the region of 500g for 14–16h/day are necessary.

Implants have been adopted in orthodontics to provide skeletal anchorage, to ↓ need for patient compliance. This has ↑ the envelope in terms of the severity of malocclusions that can be treated by orthodontics alone. Currently the term TAD is in vogue, but mini-implants and bone anchorage devices (BADs) are also used (Table 4.2). Success rates of 86.5% have been reported.
Most operators load the screws immediately. The osseointegrated type requires a latent period for integration. Need to avoid excess force levels (<250g).
Root damage—evidence suggests that if the root is perforated, then healing by cementum occurs.

Cases have been reported where damage to the eye as a result of headgear has resulted in loss of vision. For this reason, headgear should only be used by those who have received training and to avoid injury to the face, it should only be used in conjunction with two safety mechanisms which prevent displacement &/or recoil of the facebow. If eye injury should occur, immediate referral to an ophthalmologist is required.

coreTruths.title: Early detection in the developing dentition prevents bigger problems later
coreTruths.broaderContext: A handful of mixed-dentition findings, caught at the right age, can be cheap to manage and brutal if missed. Screening every recall is the lowest-cost orthodontics there is.
coreTruths.body:
## Palpate for the upper canine from age 9

From age 9 onward, palpate for the upper canine in the buccal sulcus until it erupts. A definite hollow or asymmetry between sides warrants further investigation [1]. Palatally displaced canines occur in up to 2% of patients, bilaterally in 17 to 25% [2]. Most do not erupt spontaneously, so hopeful watching ends with an older patient who has less appetite for the long treatment that follows [3]. Unerupted canines can also resorb incisor roots through a head-on collision, and that is a refer-quickly situation [4].

## A six-month rule for failure of eruption

Failure of a tooth to appear more than six months after the contralateral has erupted should ring alarm bells [5]. Eruption sequence matters at every visit during the mixed dentition phase [5].

## Balance Cs, do not balance Es or sound 6s

Unilateral loss of a primary canine in a crowded mouth shifts the centre line, and correcting that usually means fixed appliances. So loss of Cs is balanced (extract the contralateral) to prevent it [6]. Es behave differently: if an E goes early, the 6 drifts forward and that is harder to undo, so try to defer E loss until the 6s are in occlusion and do not balance or compensate [6]. Balancing a sound 6 against a poor 6 is also inadvisable; deal with each side on its merits [7].

## Median diastema usually closes on its own

Diastema prevalence drops from 98% at age 6 to 49% at 11 to 7% at 12 to 18 [8]. The standard approach before 3s erupt is review if the diastema is under 3 mm, since it usually closes as the canines come down [9]. After 3s have erupted, orthodontic closure has high relapse and needs prolonged retention. Composite additions or veneers are often a cleaner answer [9].

## Some findings need referral, not observation

The early mixed dentition refer-list is short and worth knowing: delayed eruption of permanent incisors, impaction or failure of eruption of 6s, 6s of poor long-term prognosis, severe Class III for protraction facemask, anterior crossbites compromising periodontal support, ectopic maxillary canines, and pathology like cysts [10].

citations.quote: From age 9yrs onwards and until they erupt, palpate for 3 in the buccal sulcus. A definite hollow &/or asymmetry warrants further investigation.
Up to 2%. Occurs bilaterally in 17–25% of cases. F > M.

The majority of palatally displaced canines, however, do not erupt spontaneously, so hopeful watching and waiting may only result in an older patient who is less willing to undergo the prolonged Rx required to align the displaced tooth.

Unerupted and impacted canines can cause resorption of incisor roots. For this to occur, a ‘head-on’ collision between the two seems to be required. If detected on a radiograph, a specialist opinion should be sought, quickly.
Keep the eruption sequence in mind (…… Failure of/delayed eruption, p. 66). Failure of a tooth to appear >6 months after the contralateral tooth has erupted should ring alarm bells.

In a crowded mouth, the adjacent teeth will move round into the extraction space, therefore, unilateral loss of a C (and to a lesser degree a D) will result in a centre-line shift. This is also seen when a C is prematurely exfoliated by an erupting 2. As correction of a centre-line discrepancy often involves FAs, prevention is better than cure, so loss of Cs should always be balanced. If Es are lost, the 6 will migrate forward. This is particularly marked if it occurs before eruption of the permanent tooth, so if extraction of an E is unavoidable try to defer until after the 6s are in occlusion and do not balance or compensate.
Balancing with extraction of a corresponding sound 6 is inadvisable; better to deal with other side of arch on its merit.
Prevalence 6yr-olds = 98%, 11yr-olds = 49%, 12–18yr-olds = 7%.

Before 3 erupted: if diastema <3mm—review after eruption of canines as will probably ↓ unaided. If >3mm—may need to approximate incisors to provide space for canines to erupt, but care is required not to resorb roots of 2|2 against crowns of 3|3. Requires FA and prolonged retention.

Delayed eruption of the permanent incisors. Impaction or failure of eruption of the 6s. 6s of poor long-term prognosis. Severe Class III skeletal problems suitable for orthopaedic Rx with protraction facemask. Anterior crossbites (Xbites) which compromise periodontal support. Ectopic maxillary canines. Patients with medical problems where monitoring of the occlusion would be beneficial. Pathology, e.g. cysts.

coreTruths.title: Retention is part of the plan, not an afterthought — without it, results drift back
coreTruths.broaderContext: Teeth that have been moved want to move back. Pretending otherwise is the fastest way to disappoint a patient who has worn braces for two years.
coreTruths.body:
## Retention is included in the plan from the start

Retention is part of the overall treatment package and is presented to the patient up front, including the need for compliance with retention appliances [1]. Many orthodontists now plan for long-term retention as the default [1]. The reason is simple: tooth positions are held by the same soft-tissue and occlusal forces that shaped the original malocclusion, and removing the appliance does not remove those forces.

## Stability follows the rules of the soft-tissue envelope

Proclining lower incisors out of the soft-tissue envelope is unstable [2]. Bilateral crossbite correction can partially relapse to a unilateral crossbite with displacement, so it is approached cautiously [3]. Rapid maxillary expansion is over-corrected by about 50% because the teeth relapse under soft-tissue pressure [4]. Each of these is a specific case of the same idea: the teeth go back toward whatever the soft tissues, occlusion, and skeletal pattern want.

## A positive overbite is the cheapest retainer in Class III

In Class III, an increased overbite is advantageous because it helps to retain the corrected incisor relationship [5]. So overbite reduction is avoided in Class III, and proclination of the ULS, which reduces overbite, is balanced against retroclination of the LLS, which increases it [6]. Whether the patient can achieve an edge-to-edge contact at assessment is one of the prognostic markers for whether correction will hold [7].

## Stable overbite reduction needs an occlusal stop and a smaller inter-incisal angle

Overbite reduction holds better when the inter-incisal angle is reduced and an occlusal stop prevents the lowers re-erupting [8]. Favourable growth helps because it compensates for the molar extrusion that drove the reduction in the first place [8]. Without those, molars re-intrude under occlusal forces and the bite re-deepens [9].

citations.quote: Retention of the final result should be included in the Rx plan and the need for compliance with wearing retention appliances explained to the patient. Many orthodontists now plan for long-term retention.
Proclination of lower incisors. Movement of the lower incisors from their position of stability within the soft tissue envelope is unstable in most cases.
Correction of a bilateral Xbite should be approached with caution, because partial relapse may result in the teeth occluding cusp to cusp and development of a unilateral Xbite with displacement.
Large forces are required to accomplish this—the screw is turned 0.2mm twice a day for about 2 weeks. Over-expansion is necessary as the teeth relapse about 50% under soft tissue pressure.
In Class III cases an ↑ o/b is advantageous as this will help to retain the corrected incisor position.
Amount of overbite. Need a positive o/b to retain corrected incisor position at the end of Rx. Remember that proclination of ULS will ↓ o/b and retroclination of LLS will ↑ o/b.
Can patient achieve an edge-to-edge contact of the incisors? If so this ↑ prognosis for correction of incisor relationship.

Stability of o/b ↓ is enhanced by: Reducing the inter-incisal angle and creating an occlusal stop to prevent the lower incisors over-erupting. Favourable growth as this compensates for molar extrusion. Eliminating or reducing the aetiological factors but ↓ LFH and high lower lip line can only be altered if growth is favourable.

Extrusion/eruption of molars. Passive eruption of lower molars occurs when a URA incorporating a bite plane is worn. Active extrusion of molars in either arch is possible using FAs. However, unless the patient grows vertically to accommodate this ↑ dimension, the molars will re-intrude under the forces of occlusion once appliances are withdrawn. This approach is of limited value in adults.
